reason: The sources provide 16 cross-referenced claims from multiple independent organizations including NASA, ESO, and major scientific journals, supporting a detailed 45-second script about the 2011 discovery and the billions of starless worlds.
story: The Milky Way is a cosmic graveyard for billions of orphan worlds drifting through the total darkness of interstellar space. Known as rogue planets, these nomadic objects are not bound to any star, wandering the galaxy in solitude. Astronomers first identified a massive population of them in 2011 by observing how their gravity warps space-time, a phenomenon called microlensing. These worlds are essentially invisible, emitting no light or heat, yet they likely outnumber the planets that actually have suns. Recent research suggests they might even outnumber star-bound worlds by six to one. While many are gas giants like Jupiter, researchers have recently discovered rocky rogues as small as Earth and Mars. Most were likely kicked out of their original solar systems by the gravitational bullying of larger planets during formation. Others may have formed alone from collapsing gas clouds. As upcoming missions like NASA’s Roman telescope begin their search, they may reveal that our galaxy is more populated by these lonely wanderers than by stars.
angle: Rogue planets are so common they likely outnumber star-orbiting worlds by six to one, meaning trillions of invisible worlds are wandering the dark void between the stars.

claims.claim: Rogue planets are interstellar objects of planetary mass that are not gravitationally bound to any star or brown dwarf.
These objects are also frequently referred to as free-floating planets (FFPs) or isolated planetary-mass objects.
There may be billions to trillions of rogue planets drifting through the Milky Way galaxy alone.
A landmark 2011 study used microlensing to identify ten candidates for Jupiter-mass rogue planets.
The 2011 study utilized the 1.8-metre MOA-II telescope in New Zealand and a telescope in Chile.
Microlensing occurs when the gravity of a massive object warps space-time, magnifying the light of a distant background star.
Microlensing signals from rogue planets are brief, typically lasting between a few hours and a couple of days.
Rogue planets can form within a planetary system and be later ejected into interstellar space.
Some rogue planets can form independently from the direct gravitational collapse of cold gas clouds.
Rogue planets likely outnumber planets that are bound to stars in the Milky Way.
One study suggests that rogue planets outnumber star-bound worlds by a ratio of roughly six to one.
Small rogue planets are more likely to be ejected because they are not tethered as strongly to their host stars.
Astronomers have detected an Earth-mass rogue planet candidate named OGLE-2016-BLG-1928.
A group of at least 70 rogue planets was discovered in the Upper Scorpius and Ophiuchus star-forming regions.
Young rogue planets can be directly imaged because they remain hot enough to glow for a few million years after formation.
NASA's upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is expected to discover hundreds of new rogue planets.

disputed: The exact ratio of rogue planets to star-bound planets varies between sources, with one suggesting a 6-to-1 ratio while others offer lower conservative estimates; the script should attribute the 6-to-1 figure to recent research.

The dominant formation model is debated; some researchers believe core accretion cannot produce enough giant planets to account for the rogue population, while others argue finding terrestrial-mass rogues supports the core accretion model.
